codex.summary: The GPU that started the deep-learning datacenter era: Volta with the first Tensor Cores and NVLink fabric.
codex.explain: V100 introduced Tensor Cores for mixed-precision matrix math and 2nd-gen NVLink, letting NVSwitch tie 16 GPUs into one memory-coherent domain (DGX-2). PCIe link is actually Gen3 to the host, just below this catalog range.
tradeoffs: Only 16GB HBM2 - modern LLMs do not fit, fine for ResNet/transformer-era training only
No sparsity or FP8/FP4: peak 125 dense FP16 TFLOPS is tiny by later standards

codex.summary: Ampere workhorse that carried the 2020-2023 LLM boom: 80GB HBM2e, NVLink3, Multi-Instance GPU.
codex.explain: A100 doubled NVLink to 600 GB/s and introduced TF32/BF16 tensor paths plus MIG for slicing one GPU into isolated instances. 80GB of HBM2e was the key unlock for GPT-3-class training.
tradeoffs: Great efficiency per watt for its era, but 312 dense BF16 TFLOPS ages fast vs Hopper/Blackwell
No FP8: inference economics beaten badly by H100 and later

codex.summary: Hopper flagship and the chip the generative-AI buildout fought over through 2023-2024.
codex.explain: H100 brought FP8 tensor cores (2x BF16 throughput), 900 GB/s NVLink4 with SHARP in-network reduction, and a Transformer Engine that picks per-layer precision automatically. The 2023 shortage made it effectively allocation-gated.
tradeoffs: 700W SXM module pushes air cooling to its limit; direct-to-chip liquid becomes the comfortable path
Only 80GB: large-batch serving of 70B+ models needs H200 or tensor parallelism

codex.summary: Hopper with a memory transplant: same compute as H100 but 141GB of faster HBM3e.
codex.explain: H200 keeps the H100 die and swaps in HBM3e, lifting capacity 1.76x and bandwidth to 4.8 TB/s. That is an inference win: more KV-cache per GPU means bigger batches and more tokens per dollar.
tradeoffs: Identical training speed to H100 - you pay for memory, not FLOPs
Great bridge product while waiting for Blackwell; drops in the same HGX boards

codex.summary: A Grace Arm CPU fused to a Hopper GPU by NVLink-C2C, with coherent access to LPDDR5X and HBM.
codex.explain: GH200 packages 144GB HBM3e on the GPU plus ~480GB of LPDDR5X on Grace, connected by a 900 GB/s chip-to-chip link so the GPU sees CPU memory without PCIe copies. NVLink Switch fabric builds the NVL32 domain of 32 superchips acting like one giant GPU.
tradeoffs: Coherent unified memory removes the PCIe bottleneck for huge models, but the extra Grace CPU adds cost that pure-GPU boxes avoid
NVL32 racks are liquid-cooled only and want ~600W+ per superchip removed by CDUs

codex.summary: First Blackwell: two reticle-size dies acting as one GPU, with FP4 tensor cores and 1.8 TB/s NVLink5.
codex.explain: B200 doubles everything - 8 TB/s HBM3e, 4.5 PF dense FP8, and NVLink5 fast enough to build the 72-GPU NVL72 domain. Early racks suffered real software bring-up pain (NCCL/cuDNN tuning), which is why maturity here is below Hopper.
tradeoffs: 1000W per SXM module: air cooling works but liquid is the sane default at rack scale
FP4 only pays off with quantization-aware or post-training-quantized models; legacy BF16 code sees roughly 2x H100, not 10x

codex.summary: Blackwell Ultra: same generation tuned for inference - 288GB HBM3e and 1.5x the dense FP4 throughput.
codex.explain: B300 spends its extra transistor budget on low-precision tensor throughput and HBM capacity rather than FP8 training math. The reference NVL72 rack (GB300) pushes ~140kW per rack through liquid cold plates.
tradeoffs: 1400W TDP: air-cooled HGX variants exist but direct liquid is the intended design point
Barely moves BF16/FP8 training numbers - it is a serving chip, buy B200/GB200 or wait for Rubin to train

codex.summary: Rubin GPU package (two reticle dies of HBM4) paired with the Vera Arm CPU in the VR200 NVL144 rack.
codex.explain: Each Rubin package moves to HBM4 (~13 TB/s) and NVLink6 at 3.6 TB/s; NVIDIA counts dies, so NVL144 is 144 dies = 72 packages acting as one domain. Rack power lands near 250kW, firmly in direct-liquid territory.
tradeoffs: Rubin-generation numbers are announced roadmap specs (GTC 2025), so treat exact TFLOPS as estimates until launch
Liquid-only and ~3.5kW per package slot: halls without CDU capacity cannot host it

codex.summary: 2027 roadmap monster: four reticle dies per package, ~1TB of HBM4e, 576 dies coherent in one Kyber rack.
codex.explain: Rubin Ultra NVL576 makes 144 packages (576 dies) a single NVLink6 domain targeting ~15 exaflops of FP4 inference per rack. Everything about it - ~600kW Kyber racks, 1PB-class aggregate memory - assumes a purpose-built liquid-cooled facility.
tradeoffs: All figures are roadmap estimates; early allocation will be brutally scarce
Rack power near 600kW demands busbar + CDU infrastructure most halls simply do not have

codex.summary: Ada Lovelace PCIe workhorse: cheap FP8 inference and fine-tuning without NVLink or HBM.
codex.explain: L40S pairs a pro-graphics-class GPU with 48GB of ordinary GDDR6 on a 350W air-cooled card that fits any server. With no NVLink it scales out over PCIe/Ethernet, which suits inference sharding and small-batch work far better than big training runs.
tradeoffs: 864 GB/s GDDR6 is ~4x slower than HBM parts: decode-heavy LLM serving hits the memory wall early
No scale-up fabric - tensor parallelism across cards crawls through PCIe

codex.summary: The odd-duck H100: a 94GB PCIe card sold in bridged pairs with NVLink, aimed at 70B-model inference.
codex.explain: H100 NVL puts a cut-down Hopper on a 350W PCIe card with a NVLink4 bridge (600 GB/s) between two cards, so tensor-parallel serving of Llama-2-70B stays on one air-cooled node. The quirky 94GB exists to hold that model in FP8 weights plus KV-cache.
tradeoffs: 94GB across two cards finally fits 70B-class serving on standard air-cooled servers
Domain stops at 2 GPUs and clocks are below SXM - training throughput trails H100 SXM clearly

codex.summary: NVIDIA's Arm server CPU built to sit beside GPUs on NVLink-C2C instead of PCIe.
codex.explain: Grace uses 72 Neoverse V2 cores with LPDDR5X (512 GB/s) rather than costly HBM or big DDR5 banks, and attaches to a Hopper/Blackwell GPU over a 900 GB/s coherent C2C link. That coherence lets the GPU stream CPU memory directly, which is why GH200-style hosts stop being a data-movement bottleneck.
tradeoffs: LPDDR5X gives server-class bandwidth at far lower cost and power than DDR5 RDIMMs, but lower capacity ceiling
Arm ecosystem is mature for AI hosts (drivers, NCCL, containers) though some legacy x86 enterprise software will not run

codex.summary: The Rubin-generation Grace successor: 88 custom Arm cores, one Vera per Rubin package in VR200.
codex.explain: Vera rides on the same NVLink-C2C idea with roughly double the coherent link bandwidth feeding two Rubin dies. One Vera plus two Rubin GPUs forms the VR200 compute board; the rack-scale NVL144 is built from those boards.
tradeoffs: Announced roadmap part - core counts and link figures are pre-launch estimates
Still LPDDR5X-attached: bandwidth per core matters less here than keeping the GPUs' NVLink domains fed

codex.summary: AMD dual-die OAM module that powered the Frontier exascale supercomputer.
codex.explain: Two GPU chiplets linked by Infinity Fabric share 128GB of HBM2e, roughly doubling FP64 throughput versus contemporary NVIDIA parts for HPC. ROCm support was thin outside supercomputing centers, which limited commercial adoption.
tradeoffs: Excellent FP64 and HBM capacity for 2021, competitive with A100 on HPC workloads
ROCm software maturity lagged CUDA badly; many model stacks required porting
Only 4-module xGMI domains vs NVIDIA 8-GPU NVSwitch nodes

codex.summary: AMD 2023 chiplet flagship: 192GB HBM3, the first accelerator able to hold a 70B-class model on one GPU.
codex.explain: It packages GPU compute dies plus an IO die on 2.5D interposers, delivering 5.3TB/s memory bandwidth inside a full 8-GPU Infinity Fabric domain. Huge memory made it an inference favorite where model fit beats raw FLOPs.
tradeoffs: 192GB fits a 70B model in FP16 where H100 80GB cannot, slashing multi-GPU overhead
ROCm improved greatly but still trails CUDA on long-tail kernels
750W OAM pushes many chassis toward liquid cooling

codex.summary: Mid-gen MI300X refresh that doubles memory to 256GB of faster HBM3e on the same compute silicon.
codex.explain: Same CDNA3 compute with 256GB at 6TB/s, aimed at inference density: more and bigger models resident per GPU. FLOPs are unchanged from MI300X.
tradeoffs: 256GB holds roughly 140B parameters in FP16 on a single card
No compute uplift, so bandwidth-bound token generation gains the most
1kW OAM largely forces liquid-cooled trays

codex.summary: AMD 2025 flagship: 256GB HBM3e at 8TB/s with double the compute plus FP4/FP6 support.
codex.explain: A bigger die in the same packaging doubles dense FP8 to about 5.2 PFLOPS and adds 4- and 6-bit datatypes for cheap token generation. Its 1.4kW TDP makes it liquid-cooled only.
tradeoffs: 8TB/s HBM3e is class-leading decode bandwidth for MoE serving
FP4/FP6 support targets the same quantized workloads as Blackwell
1.4kW requires DLC or immersion; air cooling is out

codex.summary: AMD CDNA4 accelerator for the Helios rack: 432GB HBM4 at about 20TB/s inside a 72-GPU UALink domain.
codex.explain: Rather than compete board by board, MI400 ships as part of the rack-scale Helios system: 72 GPUs plus MI450 host CPUs linked by UALink, with Ultra Ethernet for scale-out. Volume availability is slated for H2 2026 with OpenAI as anchor customer.
tradeoffs: 72-GPU UALink domain mirrors NVL72-style scale-up memory semantics
HBM4 capacity and bandwidth lead the 2026 generation on paper
Rack-scale procurement: you buy the Helios system, not loose cards

codex.summary: Tenstorrent dual-Wormhole PCIe card: cheap RISC-V+Tensix chips that network over plain Ethernet.
codex.explain: Two Wormhole chips expose 100GbE mesh links straight from the package, so scale-up and scale-out use the same standard Ethernet switches. It was sold near cost to seed an open software community.
tradeoffs: Ethernet-native fabric means cheap whitebox switches and no proprietary lock-in
GDDR6 (24GB) and modest FLOPs limit it to small models and experimentation
Young TT-Metalium stack requires hands-on kernel work

codex.summary: Tenstorrent second-gen single-chip card: 32GB LPDDR5, about 197 BF16 TFLOPS and 16 integrated 400GbE ports.
codex.explain: Blackhole drops dependence on a host CPU (RISC-V cores on package) and wires Ethernet into every chip, so each card is simultaneously compute and network. It targets cost-per-token inference and research clusters.
tradeoffs: 400GbE on-package removes NIC cost and enables free-form topologies
LPDDR5 bandwidth (0.5TB/s) is far below HBM parts: decode-heavy workloads only
Ecosystem and compiler still maturing vs CUDA/ROCm

codex.summary: Tenstorrent 4U server packing 32 Wormhole chips (768GB GDDR6) pre-meshed over integrated Ethernet.
codex.explain: A Galaxy is roughly 5.4 BF16 PFLOPS in a box whose chips form a 2D mesh using on-die 100GbE links; up to four Galaxies mesh into a 128-chip pod. It demonstrates Tenstorrent thesis that lossless-Ethernet scale-up can replace exotic fabrics.
tradeoffs: One box is a 32-chip domain with no separate switch purchase
GDDR6 capacity and bandwidth cap per-chip model sizes
Main risk is software (TT-Metalium/TT-NN), not hardware

codex.summary: Cerebras wafer-scale engine: a single 900k-core chip the size of a dinner plate with 44GB of on-wafer SRAM.
codex.explain: WSE-3 keeps activations in SRAM at 21PB/s and streams weights from external MemoryX, so one wafer trains or serves giant models without sharding. Clusters scale to 2048 CS-3 systems with near-linear deterministic scaling.
tradeoffs: Dataflow SRAM architecture gives extreme tokens/s per watt for decoding
Only 44GB on-wafer: weights live in MemoryX, a proprietary streaming tier
Custom stack: you adapt workloads to Cerebras, not the reverse

codex.summary: Intel Habana-built 2022 challenger: 96GB HBM2e with 24 integrated 100GbE RoCE ports per card.
codex.explain: Gaudi 2 put the network on the accelerator: scale-up and scale-out run over standard Ethernet/RoCE with no separate NICs. MLPerf results showed real training capability at aggressive prices.
tradeoffs: Integrated RoCE fabric cuts system cost and cabling complexity
SynapseAI lacked CUDA breadth, so adoption stayed niche
FP8 support exists but tooling trailed NVIDIA

codex.summary: Intel 2024 Gaudi update: 128GB HBM2e, about 1.8 FP8 PFLOPS and 24 integrated 200GbE RoCEv2 ports.
codex.explain: It doubles Gaudi 2 memory bandwidth and compute while keeping the Ethernet-native design in standard OAM packaging. Intel positioned it on price-performance for inference-heavy deployments.
tradeoffs: 24x200GbE on-package gives huge east-west bandwidth with cheap switches
SynapseAI software remains the adoption bottleneck
Roadmap uncertainty after Intel strategy shifts

codex.summary: Groq deterministic tensor-streaming LPU: 230MB of on-die SRAM, no HBM, compiler-scheduled execution.
codex.explain: The LPU executes a pre-planned schedule with no caches or memory contention, making batch-1 token latency extreme and perfectly predictable. Models are sharded across hundreds of chips wired in a rigid chip-to-chip fabric.
tradeoffs: SRAM-only design delivers outstanding decode latency and tokens/s per user
230MB per chip means weights must be sharded: 70B models span hundreds of LPUs
Great at inference serving, essentially unusable for training

codex.summary: AMD Zen4 server CPU flagship: 96 cores, 12-channel DDR5 and 128 PCIe 5.0 lanes.
codex.explain: Genoa made x86 GPU hosts cheaper per core than Intel while doubling memory bandwidth for data staging. The SP5 platform it introduced is used by most MI300 and Gaudi systems.
tradeoffs: 128 Gen5 lanes feed multiple accelerators and NICs from one socket
12-channel DDR5 must be fully populated or bandwidth tanks
High core count at modest clocks: also great for storage/frontend nodes

codex.summary: AMD Zen5 server generation: up to 192 cores per socket on the same SP5 DDR5 platform.
codex.explain: Turin (EPYC 9005) doubles cores to 192 and moves to DDR5-6400 while being drop-in compatible with Genoa boards. Dense Zen5c variants target cloud hosts and AI datacenter service nodes.
tradeoffs: 192 cores amortize host cost across more GPUs per node
500W TDP flagship SKUs need serious chassis airflow
Socket-compatible with Genoa: a capacity upgrade without a platform swap

codex.summary: Dual-port 200G Ethernet/RoCE adapter that was the standard AI node NIC of the A100 era.
codex.explain: ConnectX-6 Dx moved RDMA, adaptive routing and inline IPsec/MACsec into the NIC so hosts could do line-rate RoCE without burning CPU. Rail-optimized A100 clusters wired one 200G port per GPU across 8 rails to the leaf tier.
tradeoffs: PCIe Gen4 x16 (~32 GB/s) caps useful throughput well below the 400 Gb/s line rate
No 400G per port: keeping pace with one H100 needs two ports or an upgrade

codex.summary: Dual-port 400G adapter that gives each H100 one 400G port and speaks both Ethernet/RoCE and InfiniBand NDR.
codex.explain: ConnectX-7 unified InfiniBand and Ethernet on one chip: with Quantum-2 it gets SHARP in-network collectives, with Spectrum switches it forms Spectrum-X. DGX H100 ships one CX-7 per GPU, i.e. 400 Gb/s of scale-out per GPU.
tradeoffs: 400 Gb/s per H100 is ~50 GB/s, one third of NVLink speed, so the scale-out fabric must be non-blocking
One SKU for IB and Ethernet simplifies spares, but pulls a full PCIe Gen5 x16 slot

codex.summary: Dual-port 800G adapter shipping in GB200 NVL72 racks, feeding every pair of Blackwell GPUs with 800 Gb/s scale-out.
codex.explain: Each NVL72 compute tray carries four dual-port ConnectX-8 for eight 800G uplinks, adding up to 57.6 Tb/s of scale-out per rack. With Spectrum-X it does adaptive routing and congestion control in hardware.
tradeoffs: 800G optics or active copper per port is expensive: the cable BOM can rival the switch cost
PCIe Gen5 x16 (~128 GB/s) cannot saturate both 800G ports simultaneously

codex.summary: 1.6 Tb/s per-port adapter for the Rubin era, matched to 1.6T switch silicon and PCIe Gen6 hosts.
codex.explain: ConnectX-9 doubles per-port rate to 1.6 Tb/s and steps to PCIe Gen6 so the host link no longer bottlenecks the network. Announced at GTC 2025 alongside Quantum-X and Spectrum-X photonics.
tradeoffs: Needs 1.6T optics or very short copper: link budgets explode past a few hundred meters
Early allocations stay tight through 2027; plan lead times like a launch GPU

codex.summary: A ConnectX-class 400G NIC fused with 16 Arm A78 cores: networking, storage and security run on the card.
codex.explain: The DPU turns infrastructure work into a separate compute domain by offloading OVS, IPsec, NVMe-oF and RDMA from host CPUs, isolating tenant workloads from cluster plumbing (its SDK is DOCA).
tradeoffs: Burns ~25 W and a full Gen5 x16 slot to do what a plain NIC does at half the price
Best on storage and front-end nodes; pure GPU rail nodes usually take plain ConnectX

codex.summary: Roadmap 800G DPU pairing ConnectX-8-class line rate with a much larger Arm complex for secure multi-tenant serving.
codex.explain: BlueField-4 is positioned on the NVIDIA roadmap for the Blackwell-to-Rubin window, aiming DPU-class programmability at 800 Gb/s. Specs are announced targets, not shipping silicon yet.
tradeoffs: Roadmap part: dates and specs can slip, so treat lead times as uncertain
High watts per port means dense front-end trays must plan airflow around it

codex.summary: AMD UEC-ready 800G AI NIC for MI-series clusters, built to converge on Ultra Ethernet RDMA.
codex.explain: Pollara 400 is the first NIC aimed at the Ultra Ethernet Consortium spec, staying RoCEv2-compatible so it interoperates with existing fleets while UEC software matures. It pairs with Pensando Vulcano switch silicon in AMD reference designs.
tradeoffs: UEC is young: peak performance depends on ecosystem software still landing
8x100G port flexibility matches UEC fabrics but makes cabling denser than 2x400G

codex.summary: Fourth-generation Pensando DPU with roughly double the throughput of its predecessor and P4-programmable pipelines.
codex.explain: Salina keeps the Pensando P4-programmable packet processors and adds Arm cores, aiming at OVS, TLS and IPsec offload in cloud hosts and appliances rather than GPU rail traffic.
tradeoffs: P4 pipeline skills are scarce; offload code must be written and maintained
400 Gb/s class line rate lags 800G AI NICs: this is a cloud DPU, not a scale-out AI NIC

codex.summary: Broadcom UEC-ready 800G smart NIC, the NIC-side companion to its Tomahawk and Jericho switch silicon.
codex.explain: Thor 2 targets AI backends that want Tomahawk-class merchant switches plus a multi-vendor UEC NIC instead of a single-vendor fabric, keeping the data plane open.
tradeoffs: Merchant-silicon strategy means fabric software (SONiC/UEC) is yours to integrate
Nicer ecosystem story than NVIDIA only if you can staff it; NIC software stack is newer than MOFED/DOCA

codex.summary: Dual-port 100G Intel adapter, the classic front-end and storage NIC of x86 AI nodes.
codex.explain: E810 (Ice Lake-D lineage) is everywhere in Intel servers for management, storage and East-West traffic; supporting both iWARP and RoCEv2 let Intel shops adopt RDMA without changing fabrics.
tradeoffs: PCIe Gen4 and 100G ports only: fine for front-end, wrong for GPU rail traffic
iWARP vs RoCE means two RDMA dialects in one fleet unless you standardize

codex.summary: Passive twinax copper cable for 100G links inside a rack.
codex.explain: No electronics on board: the switch SERDES drives the copper directly, so DACs cost almost nothing to run, but attenuation kills the signal past a few meters.
tradeoffs: Cheapest and lowest-power link type, but 3-5 m reach only
Stiff twinax bundles make dense ToR wiring a physical problem

codex.summary: Passive 400G copper jumper for NDR/400G leaf links within a rack.
codex.explain: At 400G the eye margins shrink, so passive twinax tops out near 2 m; anything longer in-rack must step up to ACC or AOC.
tradeoffs: Roughly a quarter of a 400G optic price at ~1 W per end
Two-meter ceiling forces the leaf switch into the same rack as the nodes

codex.summary: Active copper cable: a DSP retimer in each connector stretches 400G copper to about 4 m.
codex.explain: ACCs trade a couple of watts and dollars for reach, bridging the gap between in-rack DAC and between-rack optics.
tradeoffs: About 40% cheaper than a 400G optic with twice the reach of passive DAC
DSP adds 2-3 W per end and a small extra failure population

codex.summary: Active copper for 800G links: the default in-rack cable of NVL72-style builds.
codex.explain: At 800 Gb/s even short twinax needs retimers; ACCs put a DSP in each end and skip lasers entirely, staying far cheaper than 800G optics.
tradeoffs: Roughly a quarter the price of an 800G optic at a fraction of the power
3 m reach keeps leaves and nodes in the same row; cross-row runs need optics

codex.summary: Passive 1.6T copper jumper for CX-9-era ports, usable only within a chassis or between adjacent trays.
codex.explain: Doubling the rate again halves passive reach, so 1.6T DAC is effectively a backplane technology. This copper wall is exactly why the industry is chasing co-packaged optics.
tradeoffs: Cheapest 1.6T link but about 1 m of reach only
Copper density limits are why 1.6T fabrics lean on CPO at scale

codex.summary: Active optical cable: fiber with lasers permanently attached, terminated in copper connectors.
codex.explain: AOCs move DAC-class simplicity into the 10-30 m gap between rack-adjacent and building-scale runs, avoiding pluggable optics and dirty connectors.
tradeoffs: Cheaper and more robust than pluggable optics for fixed runs
Fixed length and no field repair: any rerig means replacing whole cables

codex.summary: 400G active optical cable for same-row and adjacent-row 400G links.
codex.explain: The AOC integrates DSPs and lasers at both ends, trading optical flexibility for a simple plug-and-go part with no connector-loss budget.
tradeoffs: Around 60-70% of a 400G optic price with none of the dirty-connector failures
30 m ceiling: past that you need pluggable DR4/FR4

codex.summary: 800G active optical cable for short rack-to-rack hops.
codex.explain: Burying the optics inside the cable avoids the 16 W pluggable-module tax and connector reliability issues, at the cost of fixed lengths.
tradeoffs: 8 W per end versus 16 W for a pluggable 800G optic
10 m ceiling and no field repair: failures swap the whole cable

codex.summary: 400G SR8 multimode transceiver: the workhorse short-reach 400G optic on OM4 fiber.
codex.explain: SR8 drives 8 parallel 50G VCSEL lanes over an MPO-16 trunk; multimode stays cheaper than single-mode but strictly distance-limited.
tradeoffs: Cheapest 400G option under 70 m with cheap multimode fiber
Past 70 m you must move to single-mode DR4; MPO-16 trunks cost more to rework

codex.summary: 400G DR4 single-mode transceiver reaching 500 m over 8-fiber MPO.
codex.explain: DR4 sends 4 parallel 100G PAM4 lanes over single-mode fiber, covering row-to-spine distances inside a building.
tradeoffs: 500 m reach covers nearly every in-building fabric hop
Parallel optics need ribbon MPO fiber plant, pricier per meter than duplex LC

codex.summary: 400G FR4 duplex single-mode transceiver for up to 2 km.
codex.explain: FR4 lambdas four 100G lanes onto one CWDM wavelength grid over ordinary duplex LC fiber, making it the default building-to-building 400G optic.
tradeoffs: Reuses any duplex LC plant: cheapest cabling per meter
2 km reach is wasted inside a hall where DR4/SR8 are cheaper per port

codex.summary: 800G SR8 multimode optic (8x100G PAM4, 70 m on OM4): the short-reach 800G standard.
codex.explain: SR8 keeps VCSEL economics at 800G by doubling lane rate to 100G PAM4; its roughly 16 W draw is why 800G switch power budgets got painful.
tradeoffs: Cheapest 800G option under 70 m
16 W per module: 64 ports add more than a kW per switch just in optics

codex.summary: 800G DR8 single-mode optic: 8 parallel 100G lanes to 500 m over MPO-16.
codex.explain: DR8 is the inside-the-building long hop for 800G fat-trees, keeping 100G-per-lane PAM4 but doubling lane count versus DR4.
tradeoffs: 500 m reach with mature 100G lane signaling
MPO-16 single-mode ribbon costs more than duplex, and 16 W per end adds up fast

codex.summary: 800G packaged as two FR4 lanes on duplex LC fiber, reaching 2 km.
codex.explain: Putting two CWDM4-style optical submodules in one OSFP module gives 800G over a normal two-fiber plant, ideal for campus-scale spines.
tradeoffs: No ribbon fiber needed: reuses existing duplex plant
Two optical submodules per port make it the priciest 800G flavor

codex.summary: 1.6T DR8 optic: 8x200G PAM4 lanes to 500 m, the first 1.6T-class transceiver.
codex.explain: Doubling lane rate to 200G PAM4 keeps the 8-lane MPO geometry of DR8 while doubling throughput for ConnectX-9 / Quantum-X / Spectrum-X generation fabrics.
tradeoffs: About 22 W per end: optics now out-draw small switches
200G lanes sit at the edge of signaling capability, so early units have tight margins

codex.summary: The passive copper harness linking GB200 compute trays to NVLink5 switch trays in an NVL72-class rack.
codex.explain: Each superchip gets 1.8 TB/s (14.4 Tb/s) across the spine, and keeping every hop under about 1.3 m of copper is exactly why a 72-GPU coherent domain is one liquid-cooled rack.
tradeoffs: Passive copper makes a 130 kW memory-coherent domain possible, and pins it to a single rack
A harness fault partitions the domain: redundancy is per-link, not per-rack

codex.summary: Heavy IEC C19/C20 jumper cord (230 V, 16 A) from PDU to server PSU.
codex.explain: One C19 circuit delivers at most about 4 kW, so high-density trays exceed cord-count sanity long before rack power does; that is why ORv3 and NVL racks moved to busbars and busway.
tradeoffs: Cord jungle above 20 kW per rack: busbar designs eliminate it entirely
IEC ratings are amp-limited; derate for hot aisles and long runs

codex.summary: Two-inch supply/return hose set with quick-disconnects linking rack manifolds to CDU loops.
codex.explain: Direct-liquid racks push 100+ kW of heat through these hoses; drips on disconnect are the operational nightmare, so loops are built N+1 with leak detection.
tradeoffs: One wet connection can trip an entire row: leak detection and dripless QDs are mandatory
About 20 m practical rack-to-CDU distance reshapes the whole floor layout

codex.summary: Ampere-generation NVSwitch chip that glues 8 A100s into one NVLink3 domain on every HGX A100 baseboard.
codex.explain: Six of these chips per baseboard crossbar the 96 NVLink3 links so all 8 GPUs reach each other at 600 GB/s each. DGX SuperPOD racks add standalone switch tiers to stitch multiple boards into one addressable fabric.
tradeoffs: Full bisection only inside the 8-GPU board - bigger domains need extra tiers, latency and cost
Fixed 400 Gb/s link rate matches Ampere; unusable with later GPU generations

codex.summary: Hopper-generation NVSwitch chip with 64 NVLink4 ports and SHARP in-network reduction.
codex.explain: Four per HGX H100 baseboard; the same silicon in standalone 1U NVLink Switch units builds SHARP trees that extend NVLink domains to SuperPOD scale. SHARP executes AllReduce-style collectives inside the fabric, cutting latency and freeing GPU cycles.
tradeoffs: SHARP gains shrink if fabric tiers are oversubscribed
Domains stay node-scale (8-32 GPUs) versus Blackwell rack-scale NVL72

codex.summary: Liquid-cooled tray of 18 NVSwitch Gen5 chips that fuses 72 Blackwell GPUs into a single memory domain in GB200/GB300 NVL72 racks.
codex.explain: Each GPU connects at 1.8 TB/s bidirectional through a copper backplane, giving 130 TB/s all-to-all bandwidth with in-fabric collectives. Two trays per NVL72 replace the entire top-of-rack switch concept for scale-up.
tradeoffs: The only way to get NVLink domains larger than one HGX board for Blackwell
Copper backplane reach confines the domain to one rack; power and price are rack-BOM scale

name: NVLink Switch Tray Gen6 (Vera Rubin NVL144)

codex.summary: Sixth-generation NVLink switch tray for Vera Rubin NVL144, roughly tripling rack-scale NVLink bandwidth.
codex.explain: Rubin dies connect at ~2.6 TB/s each over NVLink6, enabling 144-GPU single domains that giant MoE expert-parallel training wants. Ships on the announced 2026 roadmap as part of the VR200 NVL144 rack.
tradeoffs: Roadmap part: dates and pricing carry real schedule risk
Requires liquid-cooled MGX racks; cannot retrofit into air-cooled halls

codex.summary: Quantum-2 InfiniBand switch: 64x 400G NDR ports in 1U, the backbone of 2022-2025 AI training fabrics.
codex.explain: 25.6 Tb/s of RDMA with SHARP in-network collectives, adaptive routing and self-healing failover. It carried the GPT-4-generation clusters, where optics often cost as much as the switch itself.
tradeoffs: Lowest tail latency for collectives, but InfiniBand is a niche fabric with scarce ops talent
400G optics/DAC BOM can add 50-100% on top of switch capex

tradeoffs: Enables 3-4x air-cooled rack density
Needs a CDU and facility water loop; leaks become an operational risk

codex.summary: Pad-mounted medium-voltage transformer stepping the utility 10-25 kV feed down to 400/480 V.
codex.explain: Nearly every IT watt flows through this iron, so even 1.2% copper and core loss becomes ~30 kW of heat at full load. Adding transformer capacity is how a hall grows past a few MW.
tradeoffs: Losses and cost are always on; oversizing wastes money at partial load
The utility interconnect queue, not the transformer, is usually the real bottleneck

codex.summary: Double-size pad-mount transformer for multi-MW halls and campus substations.
codex.explain: Bigger cores run slightly more efficiently per kVA and halve the count of interconnection points. Utilities often prefer fewer, larger banks.
tradeoffs: A single 5 MVA unit is one big fault domain; critical halls go 2N
Specialty craning and splicing stretch installs past half a year in practice

codex.summary: Low-voltage metal-clad switchgear lineup distributing 400/480 V to UPSs, busways and mechanical plant.
codex.explain: The protection and metering backbone: breakers, feeders and the automatic transfer logic that signals gensets when utility voltage sags. ~0.5% bus losses.
tradeoffs: Dual-bus (2N) lineups double cost but allow maintenance with zero downtime
Arc-flash domains: live work is regulated, planned and expensive

codex.summary: 500 kW double-conversion UPS keeping sags, spikes and outages away from the IT load.
codex.explain: The inverter continuously regenerates clean AC from batteries, burning ~3% of everything that passes through. Batteries bridge the seconds until diesels synchronize.
tradeoffs: Double conversion protects best but taxes every IT watt ~3%
Eco-mode reaches ~99% efficiency by passing raw utility most of the time

codex.summary: Modular 225 kW UPS frame with plug-in power modules for small halls and edge sites.
codex.explain: Buy capacity in 25-50 kW slices as the hall fills instead of paying for an oversized frame on day one. Internal N+1 modules keep the load alive during swaps.
tradeoffs: Higher cost per kW than monolithic megawatt frames
225 kW is one AI rack soon after 2023 - plan to outgrow it

codex.summary: 1.25 MW monolithic double-conversion UPS for serious halls.
codex.explain: One frame carries a megawatt-class room; paralleling frames gives N+1 redundancy at ~97% efficiency at high load. The workhorse of colo halls.
tradeoffs: N+1 paralleling nearly doubles footprint and cost
Efficiency drops badly below ~40% load - size frames to run hot

codex.summary: 2024-generation 1.25 MW UPS packing a megawatt into about half the traditional footprint at 97.5%.
codex.explain: Denser power electronics and live-swap modules shrink the power room right when AI halls need the space back for cooling kit.
tradeoffs: Concentrating 1.25 MW per frame makes maintenance windows high-stakes
Premium price only pays back when actually loaded near capacity

codex.summary: Valve-regulated lead-acid strings giving a UPS 5-10 minutes of ride-through.
codex.explain: Cheap per kWh and boring in a good way; covers the gap between utility loss and diesel sync. Round-trip losses are irrelevant for this duty.
tradeoffs: 3-5 year replacement cycle and heavy derating in warm rooms
A tonne per ~100 kWh: floor loading adds up fast

name: Vertiv DynaFlex LFP BESS (750 kW / 1.5 MWh)

codex.summary: Lithium-iron-phosphate battery cabinet pairing with Vertiv UPSs for long ride-through and peak shaving.
codex.explain: LFP lasts 2-3x longer than VRLA, tolerates deep cycling, and can shave utility demand peaks. Integrated battery management talks to the UPS lineup.
tradeoffs: Higher capex per kWh than lead-acid, though lower TCO
Thermal-runaway engineering and commissioning add real overhead

name: Vertiv PowerBar Overhead Busway (400 kW run)

codex.summary: Overhead busway run at 400 V carrying ~400 kW per tap-off zone.
codex.explain: Rack PDUs clamp onto the bus instead of pulling home-run conduits back to floor PDUs, turning rack power changes into a plug-in job.
tradeoffs: Retrofitting tap-offs under live load is slow and procedure-heavy
Tap-off boxes cost more per rack than hardwired whips

name: Vertiv Geist Switched Rack PDU (5 kW 1-phase)

codex.summary: Metered, per-outlet-switchable single-phase rack PDU for classic air-cooled racks.
codex.explain: Branch metering feeds your DCIM data and remote power cycling saves a truck roll. At 208 V single phase you top out near 5 kW per feed.
tradeoffs: Single-phase feeds cap at ~5 kW: useless for AI racks
Per-outlet switching costs 2-3x a dumb strip

codex.summary: Three-phase 400/415 V rack PDU delivering ~22 kW into one cabinet.
codex.explain: Three phases share neutral current efficiently, quadrupling per-feed power versus single-phase. The default for dense 2U-server and HGX-class racks.
tradeoffs: Requires balanced phases or you waste a third of the capacity
Still short of the 40-130 kW modern liquid racks demand

name: Vertiv Geist High-Density Rack PDU (150 kW)

codex.summary: Busbar-fed three-phase rack PDU rated 150 kW for NVL72-class liquid racks.
codex.explain: A GB200 NVL72 rack can pull 120-132 kW, several times what any corded PDU can feed; these units tap rack busbars and meter every branch.
tradeoffs: A single feed failure bricks the whole rack, so designs go A/B busbar
Only meaningful with liquid cooling: no air rack survives this density

name: Delta ORv3 Power Shelf (33 kW, 48 VDC)

codex.summary: Open Rack v3 power shelf rectifying 415 VAC to 48 VDC busbars, 33 kW per shelf.
codex.explain: ORv3 moves conversion into the rack: hot-swap 5.5 kW modules feed 48 V busbars that trays clip onto directly. NVIDIA MGX racks stack shelves to 100 kW+.
tradeoffs: 48 V means enormous currents: 100 kW draws over 2000 A through busbars
N+1 modules per shelf trade idle capacity against single-module failures

codex.summary: 2.5 MW medium-speed diesel generator set carrying the hall through utility outages.
codex.explain: Starts, warms and synchronizes in well under a minute while UPS batteries hold the load. ~38% of fuel energy becomes electricity; the rest is heat out the radiator and exhaust.
tradeoffs: Emissions permits and fuel storage make these backup-only in practice
Weekly no-load exercising is mandatory or they fail when needed

codex.summary: Industrial gas turbine generating 15 MW on-site where the grid is weak, slow or expensive.
codex.explain: Turns a gas contract into firm power for a whole AI block, and exhaust heat can drive absorption chillers in combined cooling and power mode.
tradeoffs: Gas prices flow straight into opex per kWh
An 18-month build makes this a strategic bet, not a quick fix

codex.summary: Jet-engine-derivative turbine delivering 32 MW with fast start and ~39% efficiency.
codex.explain: Aero cores spin up in ~10 minutes, letting datacenters use them for peak shaving and grid-constrained expansion, not just emergency backup.
tradeoffs: Highest capex per kW in the plant; needs firm gas supply contracts
Maintenance counts in fired hours, so cycling it daily gets costly

name: Utility Solar PPA Block (10 MW nameplate)

codex.summary: Power purchase agreement block: 10 MW of nameplate solar contracted at a fixed price, no capex.
codex.explain: You pay an interconnection fee and a per-kWh rate below grid retail. The efficiency figure models firm capacity: nights and weather mean only ~25% of nameplate is dependable.
tradeoffs: Cheapest energy per kWh but never firm: needs BESS or turbines behind it
Multi-year contract locks pricing against future market swings

codex.summary: Computer-room air handler pulling hot return air through chilled-water coils and blowing ~22 C supply.
codex.explain: Fan power is what you pay here; the real electric bill sits in the chiller plant behind the coils. EC fans and raised-floor delivery define classic hall cooling.
tradeoffs: Only as good as its chilled-water plant: count both in PUE
Air delivery caps out near 20-40 kW per rack before fans and recirculation win

codex.summary: Floor-standing 300 kW chilled-water CRAH with EC fans and variable-capacity control.
codex.explain: Larger frames with modulating fans hold supply temperature tightly across load swings, which keeps efficiency near its 22 W/kW rating most of the year.
tradeoffs: Fewer, bigger units reduce fan count but concentrate failure domains
Still air: the per-rack density ceiling remains

codex.summary: Rooftop-style modular air handling unit moving 1 MW of hall heat to a chilled-water loop.
codex.explain: Central airhandlers beat rows of small CRAHs on fan efficiency at scale and free-cool on economizer dampers when outside air cooperates.
tradeoffs: Ducting and volume dampers make retrofits disruptive
One 1 MW unit down means a hot zone until N+1 kicks in

codex.summary: Passive chilled-water rear-door heat exchanger neutralizing rack exhaust before it reaches the room.
codex.explain: The door coil captures 100% of rack heat with no added fans, so the room loop only sees leakage and lighting. A cheap bridge from air-cooled to high density.
tradeoffs: Adds ~30 kg and door swing depth to every cabinet
Capacity collapses if chilled water is not cold and plentiful

codex.summary: Fan-assisted rear-door heat exchanger extracting up to 60 kW from a single rack.
codex.explain: Assisted doors add small fans to pull exhaust through a bigger coil, pushing past passive-door limits while still keeping room air thermally neutral.
tradeoffs: Fan power (9 W/kW) is still far cheaper than CRAH overcooling
Door fans become a maintenance item at thousands of racks

codex.summary: In-rack coolant distribution unit pumping temperature-controlled water to cold plates.
codex.explain: Separates dirty facility water from the polished tech-coolant loop touching the silicon, exchanging heat through a plate exchanger inside the rack.
tradeoffs: One pump failure takes out exactly that rack: cheap but blunt redundancy
Rack real estate spent on the CDU is not spent on GPUs

name: CoolIT Rack Cold-Plate Loop Kit (80 kW)

codex.summary: Manifolds, quick-disconnects and copper cold plates converting a rack to direct liquid cooling.
codex.explain: Captures 70-80% of AI heat straight into water at 30 C, sidestepping the air ceiling entirely; the loop still needs a CDU to reject that heat somewhere.
tradeoffs: Accelerator swaps mean dripless disconnects and spill procedures
A fitting leak is rare but catastrophic for one tray

codex.summary: ORv3-form-factor in-rack CDU moving 150 kW from rack coolant loop to facility water.
codex.explain: Slides into the same rack ecosystem as ORv3 power shelves, giving MGX-style builds matched liquid distribution at 32 C supply.
tradeoffs: Higher supply temps save chiller energy but shrink safety margin
Still per-rack redundancy: row-level CDUs scale better

codex.summary: Row-scale 1.8 MW liquid-to-liquid CDU sized for GB200 NVL72-class rows.
codex.explain: Two 130 kW racks already exceed 250 kW, so halls deploy megawatt CDUs between facility water and rack coolant, typically one per rack-pair with an N+1 spare.
tradeoffs: N+1 spares idle a megawatt of capital capacity
Facility water temperature and quality define real throughput

codex.summary: Redundant-pump 1.6 MW coolant distribution unit for dense direct-liquid rows.
codex.explain: Dual pump paths and warm-water operation at 32 C let rows run most of the year on dry coolers alone instead of compressor-based chillers.
tradeoffs: Built-in redundancy raises price per kW over in-rack units
Bigger single units mean bigger maintenance lifts and rigging

codex.summary: 2.3 MW coolant distribution unit sized for GB300 and Vera-Rubin era liquid rows.
codex.explain: Racks are headed past 130 kW each, and CDU capacity per row has to keep pace; 2.3 MW covers a pair of 250 kW-class racks with change to spare.
tradeoffs: A single 2 MW+ unit is a huge blast radius without row redundancy
High supply temps save chillers but must match silicon warranty limits

codex.summary: Self-contained air-cooled screw chiller making 400 kW of 10 C chilled water, no cooling tower needed.
codex.explain: Rejects hall heat straight to outside air via refrigeration at roughly 1.1 kW per ton, which lands near 290 electrical watts per kW of IT heat.
tradeoffs: Simple siting, but capacity and efficiency sag badly on hot days
Compressor power dominates PUE: pair with economizer hours when possible

codex.summary: Plant-class water-cooled centrifugal chiller delivering 2 MW of chilled water at ~0.6 kW per ton.
codex.explain: Condenser water from towers lets centrifugal compressors hit ~170 W/kW, the efficient end of chilled-water plants that large halls standardize on.
tradeoffs: Needs towers, water treatment and permits on site
Part-load efficiency favors staging several smaller units

codex.summary: 1 MW dry cooler rejecting warm loop heat to ambient air with fans only, no compressor.
codex.explain: With 30 C+ direct-liquid loops, the loop runs warmer than the outside air most of the year, so plain radiators do the job and chillers stay off.
tradeoffs: Capacity collapses on 40 C days: size for your design ambient
Zero water use, but you trade that against hot-weather derating

codex.summary: Evaporative cooling tower rejecting 2 MW of condenser heat at ~12 W/kW.
codex.explain: Evaporating 1 kg of water absorbs ~2.26 MJ, so towers reject heat nearly free electrically; they are what makes water-cooled chillers and water-side economization efficient.
tradeoffs: Burns roughly 1.8 L of water per kWh of heat rejected
Legionella dosing, winterization and drift elimination never stop

codex.summary: Single-phase immersion tank: ~100 kW of servers bathed in circulating dielectric fluid.
codex.explain: Boards sit in non-conductive oil that convects heat to a 40 C water loop; fans disappear entirely and silicon can run nearer its limits.
tradeoffs: PUE contribution near 1.03-1.05, but hardware swaps are slow and oily
Several tonnes filled: floor loading and specialist ops skills required

codex.summary: Megawatt-scale immersion pod running 45 C warm-water heat rejection for dense AI blocks.
codex.explain: Purpose-built multi-tank pods with integrated pumps target the densest deployments without cold plates, feeding heat straight to dry coolers or reuse.
tradeoffs: Locks you into immersion-compatible tray designs
Immersion technicians are rare; train and retain them

codex.summary: Single-slot, 72 W inference card that fits 1U servers.
codex.explain: Passively cooled and tiny, the L4 is the density king for small-model serving, video and embeddings. It has no NVLink and only 24 GB, so large LLMs do not fit.
tradeoffs: Best tokens per watt for small models
24 GB caps model size; no scale-up

codex.explain: Half an A100 with HBM bandwidth, so memory-bound inference runs well. NVLink bridge pairs two cards, but nothing larger.

Small memory, bridge-only scale-up

codex.explain: Same die with fewer SMs and HBM2e, in a standard double-width card that fits any 4U/2U PCIe server. Great for inference; for training you give up NVLink4 and ~35% memory bandwidth.

No NVSwitch: tensor-parallel scaling is weak

codex.summary: 96 GB GDDR7 Blackwell workstation/server card with FP4.
codex.explain: Big memory for the money with FP4 support, a strong cost-per-token option for mid-size models. GDDR7 bandwidth is far below HBM, so decode throughput lags datacenter parts.
tradeoffs: Lowest $/GB of fast memory
GDDR bandwidth limits long-context decode

codex.summary: CDNA2 PCIe card with 64 GB HBM2e and 1.6 TB/s.
codex.explain: The air-cooled AMD alternative for PCIe servers; strong FP64 for HPC, cheaper than A100 but with a thinner software ecosystem.
tradeoffs: Good memory capacity per dollar
ROCm maturity trails CUDA

codex.summary: Hopper with compute cut ~85% but 4 TB/s HBM3 and full NVLink.
codex.explain: Built to meet export limits: tiny FLOPS, huge memory bandwidth. Terrible for training, surprisingly good for decode-heavy inference where bandwidth is the limit.
tradeoffs: Inference-only value
Compute-starved for training

codex.summary: 16-core Genoa with all 128 PCIe5 lanes at 200 W: the budget GPU-host CPU.
codex.explain: A GPU server needs lanes and memory channels, not cores. This part keeps the full I/O of Genoa at one fifth of the price of a 96-core chip, so it minimises $/GPU for inference trays.
tradeoffs: Cheapest way to get 128 Gen5 lanes
Few cores: data loading and tokenisation can bottleneck

codex.summary: 56-core Sapphire Rapids with PCIe5 and AMX: the DGX H100 host CPU.
codex.explain: Intel AMX accelerates small-batch CPU inference, and PCIe5 feeds ConnectX-7. Only 80 lanes per socket, so GPU-dense trays need two.
tradeoffs: Strong OEM support
80 lanes/socket versus 128 on EPYC

codex.summary: 128 P-cores with MRDIMM and 96 PCIe5 lanes at 500 W.
codex.explain: Granite Rapids pushes memory bandwidth past 800 GB/s with MRDIMMs, useful for CPU-hosted KV caches. Power and price are high.
tradeoffs: Huge host memory bandwidth
500 W per socket adds to rack power

codex.summary: 192 Arm cores at 350 W with 128 PCIe5 lanes.
codex.explain: Cloud-native Arm host with excellent perf/W for orchestration and data prep. x86-only software and drivers occasionally lag.
tradeoffs: Great perf per watt
Some tooling is x86-only

codex.summary: Cheap dual-port 25G OCP NIC for the front-end network.
codex.explain: Management, datasets and inference traffic rarely need 400G. A cheap NIC saves money but cannot feed GPU-to-GPU collectives.
tradeoffs: Great for front-end and inference ingress
Useless as a training back-end

codex.summary: Single-port 200G ConnectX-7 at about half the price of the 400G card.
codex.explain: Pair one per GPU in PCIe inference nodes where 200G per GPU is plenty; training clusters usually want 400G.
tradeoffs: Half the cost and power of CX7-400
Caps per-GPU network at 25 GB/s

codex.summary: Open-networking 51.2 Tb/s-class white-box switch running SONiC.
codex.explain: Hyperscalers buy white-box Tomahawk switches for half the price and run SONiC. You save capex but own the software, tuning and bug fixes.
tradeoffs: About half the price of branded Ethernet
You are your own support team

codex.summary: Workhorse 100G leaf for 2020-era Ethernet back-ends and storage.
codex.explain: Cheap and ubiquitous; enough for A100 nodes with 100G NICs, a bottleneck for anything later.
tradeoffs: Low cost per port
Out of its depth past 200G

codex.summary: Cisco Silicon One 400G router/switch for fabric and storage.
codex.explain: Deep buffers and strong telemetry. Cisco, Arista and NVIDIA Spectrum-X all aim at the AI Ethernet back-end.
tradeoffs: Operational maturity
Premium price per port

codex.summary: Out-of-band management switch for BMCs and PDUs.
codex.explain: Every server and PDU has a management port. The OOB network is how you recover a hung node without touching it.
tradeoffs: Tiny cost, vital reliability
One per rack adds up at scale

codex.summary: Swaps the hall between utility and generator.
codex.explain: Without an ATS a utility outage is a hard stop. The ATS detects loss, starts the generator and transfers when voltage is stable.
tradeoffs: Single point of failure unless duplicated
Needed for any real backup plan

codex.summary: Millisecond A/B feed transfer for dual-corded racks.
codex.explain: Lets a rack ride through a failing feed with no outage. Cheaper than full 2N, but still a single device.
tradeoffs: Cheap path to A/B redundancy
Transfers load, does not store energy

codex.summary: Overhead busway that feeds rack taps without cabling.
codex.explain: Busway makes power reconfigurable and cuts install cost per rack, but a fault can take a whole row.
tradeoffs: Fast rack adds
Fault domain is a full run

codex.summary: Lithium-ion battery cabinet for UPS ride-through.
codex.explain: Li-ion lasts 10-15 years versus 3-5 for lead-acid, takes a third of the floor space, and tolerates warm rooms. It costs about 2.5x as much up front.
tradeoffs: Lower total cost over 10 years
High upfront price and fire-safety rules

codex.summary: 3 MW diesel generator with emissions after-treatment.
codex.explain: Backs up a whole hall for days. Long lead time and strict permits; a genset that was never load-tested will not start when needed.
tradeoffs: Reliable backup
Long lead time and emissions permits

codex.summary: Utility-scale battery for peak shaving and backup.
codex.explain: Charges when power is cheap and covers peak or outages. It cuts PPA overage and demand charges but does not replace a genset for multi-hour outages.
tradeoffs: Arbitrage and demand shaving
Limited duration

codex.summary: Self-contained DX air conditioner for small rooms.
codex.explain: No chilled water needed, so it is quick to deploy, but compressor power is high (poor PUE).
tradeoffs: Easy install
Inefficient

codex.summary: EC fan-wall air handler fed by chilled water.
codex.explain: Many small fans share the load and run at partial speed, saving fan energy compared with big CRAHs.
tradeoffs: Redundant by design
Needs a chilled-water plant

codex.summary: Dry cooler with water-spray assist on hot days.
codex.explain: Free cooling most of the year; the spray uses water only during heat peaks. Warm-water DLC loops pair well with it.
tradeoffs: Very low energy per kW removed
Water use and local availability

codex.summary: Software-defined parallel filesystem on NVMe nodes.
codex.explain: Delivers hundreds of GB/s to GPU clients over RDMA. Software-licensed, so it runs on commodity servers.
tradeoffs: Fast and flexible
Licence is a recurring cost

codex.summary: All-flash scale-out file/object system.
codex.explain: Holds datasets and finished checkpoints cheaper than hot NVMe, at lower bandwidth.
tradeoffs: Cheap warm tier
Not for checkpoint bursts

codex.summary: Dense HDD node for the object tier.
codex.explain: Cold datasets and old checkpoints belong on spinning disk. Throughput is poor but cost per PB is tiny.
tradeoffs: Lowest $/PB
Slow rebuilds

codex.summary: Entry DDR5 DIMM for cost-sensitive hosts.
codex.explain: Enough for inference hosts that do not cache datasets.
tradeoffs: Cheap
Low capacity

codex.summary: 128GB DDR5 for memory-hungry hosts.
codex.explain: Useful for CPU offload and KV-cache spill; costs more per GB.
tradeoffs: High capacity per slot
Higher $/GB

codex.summary: Small boot drive for the OS image.
codex.explain: Keeps the host alive when the big drives are busy with checkpoints.
tradeoffs: Cheap
Little capacity

codex.summary: Cat 3516: the classic 2.5 MW data-centre diesel standby set.
codex.explain: Caterpillar dominates datacenter standby power: Cat 3500-series sets start in about 10 seconds and take full load in one step. You need fuel storage, emissions permits and monthly load tests.
tradeoffs: Proven, fast start, strong dealer service
Diesel permits and fuel logistics

codex.summary: Cat C175-16: 3 MW Tier-2 diesel set for large halls.
codex.explain: More power per engine means fewer sets and a simpler paralleling plant.
tradeoffs: Fewer engines to parallel
Long lead time

codex.summary: Gas-fired prime-power set: no diesel tank, can run continuously.
codex.explain: Gas sets can run as on-site prime power and sell flexibility to the grid; they depend on pipeline gas, so a gas outage is a power outage unless you hold diesel too.
tradeoffs: Continuous duty and lower emissions
Depends on gas pipeline

codex.summary: Cummins QSK95: 3.5 MW high-speed diesel set.
codex.explain: Cummins is the main alternative to Cat. Price and lead time vary by quarter; mixing brands complicates spares and training.
tradeoffs: Competitive price
Mixed fleets mean mixed spares

codex.summary: Rolls-Royce MTU 20V4000: a dense 2.75 MW standby set.
codex.explain: MTU sets are popular in hyperscale builds and are available in rated-for-data-centre 10-second-start versions.
tradeoffs: Compact for its rating
Smaller dealer network

codex.summary: Kohler KD2500: lower-cost 2.5 MW set with shorter lead time.
codex.explain: Often the cheapest and quickest to receive; you trade some dealer depth.
tradeoffs: Lower price, faster delivery
Less aftermarket support

name: Bloom Energy Server (300 kW SOFC fuel cell)

codex.summary: Solid-oxide fuel cell running on natural gas, no combustion.
codex.explain: Bloom boxes give always-on on-site power with no diesel and quiet running. Cost per kW is high but they avoid grid interconnection waits.
tradeoffs: Bypasses grid queue
High $/kW

codex.summary: Synchronises several generators onto one bus and transfers load automatically.
codex.explain: With more than one genset you need paralleling gear. It also gives N+1: lose one engine and the others still carry the hall.
tradeoffs: Enables N+1 genset plants
Complex controls, a single bus

codex.summary: A second grid connection from a different substation.
codex.explain: Most real outages are grid faults. A diverse second feed turns them into a non-event but takes a year of utility engineering.
tradeoffs: Cuts outage frequency sharply
Long lead time and big upfront fee

codex.summary: Rotary UPS: a spinning flywheel carries load until the generator starts.
codex.explain: No batteries to replace; ride-through is only 10-15 seconds, so it requires a generator that starts reliably.
tradeoffs: No battery maintenance
Short ride-through

codex.summary: Medium-voltage switchgear for large halls.
codex.explain: Large sites distribute at MV and step down near the load; this is the breaker line-up that makes it safe to maintain.
tradeoffs: Needed past ~5 MW
Long lead time

codex.summary: 10 MVA transformer for multi-hall campuses.
codex.explain: Transformers are the longest-lead item in power; order early.
tradeoffs: One unit powers four halls
Lead time over a year in tight markets

codex.summary: Trane Series R air-cooled screw chiller.
codex.explain: Compact and reliable. Efficiency collapses in heat waves; water-cooled plants do better at scale.
tradeoffs: Simple, no tower
Poor hot-day efficiency

codex.summary: Carrier AquaForce air-cooled chiller with VFD compressors.
codex.explain: Variable-speed compressors track load, saving energy at part load, which is where datacenters run most hours.
tradeoffs: Good part-load efficiency
Capex above fixed-speed units

codex.summary: YORK YVAA free-cooling-capable air chiller.
codex.explain: Adds a free-cooling coil so cold weather needs no compressors.
tradeoffs: Seasonal free cooling
Climate-dependent savings

codex.summary: Magnetic-bearing centrifugal chiller on a cooling-tower loop.
codex.explain: The efficiency leader for big halls, but it needs a tower, pumps and makeup water.
tradeoffs: Best kW per ton at scale
Water, tower and pumps

codex.summary: Oil-free magnetic-bearing centrifugal chiller.
codex.explain: No oil means less maintenance and better part-load efficiency.
tradeoffs: Low maintenance, great part load
Higher price

name: Trane Warm-Water Trim Chiller (1.2 MW, DLC)

codex.summary: Trim chiller for warm-water liquid cooling loops.
codex.explain: Liquid-cooled racks accept 30 C water, so the chiller only trims on the hottest days. Energy per kW removed falls dramatically.
tradeoffs: Excellent for DLC
Useless for air-cooled halls

name: Carrier AquaEdge Trim Chiller (2 MW, DLC)

codex.summary: Large warm-water trim chiller for liquid-cooled halls.
codex.explain: Pairs with dry coolers for most-year free cooling.
tradeoffs: Low PUE
DLC only

codex.summary: 10 Gb/s Tier-1 IP transit.
codex.explain: Enough to start a small inference business. Billed monthly; build-out takes weeks.
tradeoffs: Cheap to start
Single carrier means a single fiber-cut risk

codex.explain: Serves mid-size inference fleets and dataset ingestion for training.

Still a single carrier

codex.summary: 400 Gb/s IP transit.
codex.explain: For large inference fleets and multi-petabyte dataset pulls.

Large commitment

codex.summary: 400G from a third carrier for diversity.
codex.explain: The second leg of a redundant internet edge.
tradeoffs: Redundancy
Cost

tradeoffs: Low jitter, predictable
